title: Comparison of Microscopy and Image Processing Techniques to Quantify Recrystallization Fraction in HSLA Steel Grades
content: High-strength, low-alloy (HSLA) steel is widely used in automotive reinforcements and structural components due to its low cost, formability, and weldability. Grain boundary strengthening, a key mechanism in HSLA steels, is achieved by refining grain size, increasing grain boundaries, and restricting dislocation motion [1,2]. Cold rolling of the sheet steel introduces microstructural texture (i.e., grains are elongated in the rolling direction (RD)) and elevates dislocation density, which is relieved through an annealing treatment—a process comprising recovery, recrystallization, and grain growth. During the annealing process, elongated grains become ‘equiaxed’ or more circular, changing the microstructure and thereby changing properties as shown in Figure 1. Strength of the material progressively reduces with increasing annealing temperatures, whereas ductility is improved. Due to the influence of microstructure on properties, obtaining an efficient best practice method for measuring recrystallization in HSLA steel grades is valuable to develop processing-structure-property relationships in production of this grade.
